utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Good to see all of you apparently in good health. Good morning, Mr. Lukic. Madam Registrar, could you call the case. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution Douglas Stringer, Lisa Biersay, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, and interns Nicolas Hoban and Marija Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell with legal intern Paul Stokes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic on behalf of the witness who should testify today. I don't know if he's protected or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. He is not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So on behalf of Mr. Borislav Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, one administrative matter. Due to the late start we will take one break at 11.45, a 30-minute break. And then there are two very short oral rulings. First one. On 21st of March, 2014, the Prosecution filed its 15th motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On 31 March 2014, the Defence filed a response in which it opposed the motion. On the 1st of April, 2014, the Prosecution filed a request for leave to reply and a reply in which it withdrew the motion. The Chamber hereby grants the request for leave to reply and notes the withdrawal of the motion. Second one is as follows. The Trial Chamber is seized of the Prosecution motion for the substitution of Rule 65 ter admitted Exhibits P1964 and P3038, filed on 14 March. The Defence did not respond. The motion is hereby granted. The registry will take necessary measures to implement this decision by the 22nd of April, 2014, and update the Chamber and parties of its implementation. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogunovic. Thank you for coming to The Hague. Could I please ask you to state your name and date of birth for the record. And I first should ask you, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Borislav Bogunovic, born on the 25th of March, 1950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bogunovic, you are to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information. Can I now ask you to make the solemn declaration the usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Biersay, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examination by Lisa Biersay:

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you comfortably seated where you are?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could I ask you just to move a little bit closer to the microphone, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And are you able to see the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I see you're reaching for your glasses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we start looking at any documents, Mr. Bogunovic, could you describe what positions you held in the SAO SBWS government in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I was minister of the interior, from 1991, and then I was deputy prime minister in 1992. And later on, I was vice speaker of the Assembly of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it true that you provided several statements to representatives of the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You've also provided statements in local proceedings as well in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to 2012. Did you provide a statement to the representatives of the OTP in September of 2012?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you able to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In what language did you review it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You signed that statement in September 2012; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you reviewed it again in 2013, September 2013; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And again, you reviewed that statement in March of this year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now turn to tab 15, if I may ask the registry to display 65 ter number 5962. And may I have some assistance in giving Mr. Bogunovic a hard copy of this document. I've already conferred with the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogunovic, you have a hard copy of it and we are trying to find an electronic version so that it will come up on the screen, but it thought it would be helpful for you to have it in your hands as well. Now, I don't know which is better for you to see, the screen or the hard copy that's in front of you. Do you have a preference?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to the hard copy in front of you on the first page, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I signed. It contains my details, my name, surname, date and place of birth, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now you said that you recognised your name -- you recognised your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is this the September 2012 statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could simply go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And just directing -- I won't go through all the pages, but directing your attention to the bottom of that page, do you recognise anything?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the bottom of the first page?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Of -- the page that you're looking at now, do you see your initials on that page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, upon your review, the two times, of this document, you had some corrections that you wanted to be made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to paragraph 5, which is on the page you're looking at, page 2, at the very bottom. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph it describes that you had been convicted to 32 years of imprisonment for murder. Has that number changed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at this moment, the sentence is 20 years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 16, which is page 4 of the document that you're holding. And specifically, it reads: "After 2 May, the SNC held two or three meetings on the subject at Ljubija Novakovic's home in Baca Palanka." Is the word "home" correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We did that at the office, the office where Ljubo Novakovic worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to, I think it will be page 18 for the hard copy that you're holding, Mr. Bogunovic, if you could go to paragraph 89. So it's on page 18.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you look at the bottom of the page that you're looking at and tell me what page number it has written?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I have 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now if I could direct your attention to that last sentence right before paragraph 90. And it says: "We received the same blue uniforms and equipment that the MUP police of Serbia wore, trousers, jackets, short-barrelled weapons, which were red Zastava pistols calibre 65." Is the number of the calibre correct? Sir, right above paragraph 90, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of this is correct except for the calibre. It should be 7.65.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now if you could go to page 27, specifically paragraph 143 once you get there. Are you on page 27?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And paragraph 143. If you could look five lines down you'll see the word "vojsku," and my question to you is whether or not that's the correct word.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it should rather say "the Ministry of Justice," to my mind, instead of "vojska," "the army." So the Ministry of Justice along with the Ministry of the Interior, the police that had been established at the time and that could try the persons who were supposed to be tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say the word "vojska," "army," should not be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if I could read the English, that sentence reads: "That is what Susa was referring to when he said we had the police and we had judiciary ..." Is that consistent with the correction that you just made?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogunovic, with the corrections you just made, is the information contained in your statement, is that information accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today about the information you provided in that statement, would your answers - in substance - be the same?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would move for the admission of the statement, which is 65 ter number 5962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this time that would conclude my direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bogunovic, although we have met on two occasions already, for the transcript I have to introduce myself to you. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I am Defence counsel for Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. First of all, I would like you to clarify a few of the answers that you gave to the Prosecutor now and that are contained in the transcript. First of all, can you tell me when were you minister of the interior and until when, in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, in which period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the period of the establishment of our ministry, our government, that was sometime in August until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in which period were you the deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was deputy prime minister when I was replaced as minister of the interior, when I was transferred to the position of deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember which period this was when you were deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Deputy prime minister? I think I started carrying out those duties in 1991, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Say until 1992, I don't know what month. Towards the end of 1992. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in which period were you the vice-president of the Assembly of the Republic of the Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I held that position from the establishment of -- actually from the first multiparty elections in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when these multiparty elections were held?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now was it 1993 or 1994? Sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said to the Prosecutor today that you reviewed the statement before you in 2012 and then 2013 and now in March 2014.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is whether you read it carefully?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I read it. I tried to read it as it was written, but I think that I did read it properly, but it's possible that -- well, I don't know. As far as I could see all of this, perhaps I omitted a sentence or two, but I don't know whether there is anything meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how much time you devoted to reading this statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about two or two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any inconsistencies in this statement, anything that was contradictory?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not exactly about everything. It would have taken a lot longer if I went from one part to another and looked at each and every sentence, trying to see what each and every sentence meant. I didn't have all that time, and to tell you the truth, I didn't really pay attention to each and every word. But on the whole, I think that the essence is there. Now, whether there is something --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But when you say that you didn't have enough time, did you have other commitments at the time or, quite simply, were you not concentrated? Were you preoccupied with other things?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I have a big problem that I've been dealing with over the past three years, and it creates major problems for me, and I read something and a few minutes later I forget that. It's not intentional or anything like that. Quite simply, this case of mine, this thing that I'm dealing with, it brings me to that. I read something and then I'm thinking of something else. So I cannot tell you exactly now whether somewhere -- well, perhaps there are some things that are not correct. It wouldn't be anything big, but there is that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the Prosecutor's question here, you said that you were convicted to 20 years in prison. Could you just clarify this for us? Does it have anything to do with something that happened during the war or not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. The only thing that has to do with the war and things like that is that is I am not as calm as I used to be. I felt that the war has taken its toll, and at certain moments I'm more irritable than I was before. I used to be reticent before, but now I see that I get upset very easily. It's a lot easier for me to change my mood, and this affects my psyche and me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but my question is: The event on account of which you were convicted, is it something that happened during the war or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, in your statement you said -- well, it's contained in one chapter. You spoke about the establishment of the SDS and the work of the SDS, especially in Vukovar. Since you were a member of that party and you held high office in that party, first of all, I'd like to ask you why you actually became a member of that party in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I joined that party because, before that, the HDZ party had been established and it had been in power for some seven or eight months, and in the elections they had won power together with the SDP. I never thought of going into politics, but at certain moments I was bothered by this, especially at work when people were saying, "Ah, if you were not a Serb, you would have really made it in life," and so on and so forth. And then it was even more insulting when they would say, "Well, let's not take him along. We cannot speak openly, he's a Serb," and so on. So this is something that I could not understand at first. I wondered why, because until then I was on good terms with all of these people. We socialised. We were friends. We even went to one another's home. At our patron saint's day, there were always 70 per cent Croats and 30 per cent Serbs present. So I asked myself: Now, what is this that is happening now? So, I mean, at one moment, as everything was the way it was, I said, well, a Croatian party had been established and we're going to create a Serb party, and that's how I joined in the establishment of this party or, rather, the beginning of the establishment of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the beginning of the establishment of the Serb Democratic Party, are you talking about this committee in Vukovar or the party in general?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the party in general, especially in Vukovar. The party was established, Jovan Raskovic was the founder of that party. I was not present when he founded the party, but I was in Vukovar, at Adica, where there were 8- or 9.000 persons present, and Jovan Raskovic was present too. And then this rally that was held there and people were selected there who would represent the SDS in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You certainly know - and I will tell you that we have information here - about this referendum that was held by the Serb people in Croatia, in terms of whether they would stay in Yugoslavia or whether they would accept Croatia's separation from Yugoslavia. Do you remember that referendum?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the result of this referendum?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the referendum in the Serb villages, or, rather, where there were more Serbs living, it was almost 100 per cent. This was done and it was done for the purpose of seeing how the people felt, and they all wanted Yugoslavia, as it had existed until then, to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they all wanted Yugoslavia to continue, you're referring to the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the position of the Serb Democratic Party as well?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a meeting before that and this was adopted unanimously; namely, that our wish was to remain in Yugoslavia or, rather, that Yugoslavia should remain as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, we have some information also about the organisation of village guards in Serb villages at the time. Can you tell us what kind of guards these were and why they were organised in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time there were village guards along the main roads along which people passed. By then, what was noticeable was that armed people were passing by and that weapons were being transported in automobiles. At the time we did not have any guards at all. However, at the meeting a decision was taken that we should have our guards there, too, as the Croats already did have, and that there should be check-points at entrances and exits into towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards were organised by the inhabitants of particular villages; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every village held meetings and they elected their Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff was in charge. They decided who would go on guard duty, who would procure the goods that were needed, so there were people who appointed these guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, you were elected at a rally of the citizens of Negoslavci as this commander of whatever it was, the Crisis Staff, the Territorial Defence, whatever it was called, I don't know, but this is the duty that you performed; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At first I was president of the Crisis Staff, and afterwards this grew into a position called the president of the Territorial Defence; that is to say, that I discharged those duties for seven or eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, you performed these duties until you were elected minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in August?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also have information to the effect that these organs at the time, these guards, whatever we're going to call them, that they communicated between and among themselves but they did not have superior command; that is to say, that they operated at local level. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Since we were separated anyway, very often a village would be separated by one Croatian village or two Croatian villages, so it wasn't easy to communicate, and then each village, each Crisis Staff operated on its own, whatever they deemed best or, rather, what mattered the most at a particular point in time in terms of the defence of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, this situation prevailed until the army came in, until they took control of all these villages and placed all of these villages guards and the Territorial Defence, whatever it was called, all of that, these groups of people, the army placed all of these groups under their command; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say something? A bit before that, before this question, may I explain how all of this happened and all the things that we went through? I mean, I'm trying to say that in the meantime there was this visit in Vukovar. The then-minister of interior of Croatia, Mr. Boljkovac, and also the deputy prime minister of Croatia, Mr. Slavko Degoricija, they came since Goran was arrested in Plitvice at the time. They came and tried to do have the barricades, the roadblocks removed, and also to do away with these village guards and to go back to the original situation, not to have any problems, and to continue with a peaceful, regular type of life that prevailed in that area. I attended that meeting, too. I was invited. I came there and we talked as human beings, and the explanation provided was that it would not be a good things to have these barricades, these village guards and all of this, that all of that should be done away with. At first I accepted that, but I said that I could not decide that on my own. And I said to them, "I suggest to you that we go to Borovo Selo and I have is a staff there, and if that is what we agree on there, then that is what we will do and that will be done." They accepted that. We went to Borovo Selo and we were met there in the traditional Serb way, with bread and salt. We held a meeting for about an hour and a half, and ultimately we agreed that these village guards and barricades be removed. However, when we went back to Vukovar, quite simply we thought that this had been resolved. However, at my request, Mr. Mercep also, who was on the other side, he was the responsible person there, he was also invited to that meeting, and I asked whether it was possible to go to his village, too, and do the same thing, and reach agreement with them, too, to have this happen, so that the entire area of the municipality of Vukovar would observe that. And that's where there was a problem. He said that that would not be possible, that he could not guarantee our security, and that he is not in a position to make it possible for us to go there peacefully and safely, as they had come to Borovo Selo, which caused a disruption in our relations a bit. However, Mr. Degoricija persuaded us to accept this. There weren't any barricades until Goran, so this was Tuesday, and then on Thursday they promised us that they would bring Goran to see what the situation was and that's what happened. They brought Goran and there were no barricades on the Serb side. Goran returned after that. They again, for some other reasons -- well, we had exact information that, at the time, about ten of the most prominent Serbs in Vukovar went missing, that they were simply not there. And then again this thing happened; namely, there was a loss of mutual confidence. And at the time, again, these same barricades were set up. And after all of that, what you said happened; namely, the army came to this area and that then things became different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we just clarify one point. There, in Borovo Selo, when these officials of the Croatian government came and when the removal of barricades was discussed, who was it that they talked to in Borovo Selo? Was it Soskocanin?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the way it was. Borovo Selo was the biggest village. It had the largest population, about 11.000. We always tried to accept what the majority wanted. And of course, Vukasin Soskocanin was there and Vitomir Devetak and many others who were members of the Serb Democratic Party. To tell you the truth, it was accepted that these barricades should be removed throughout the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you spoke about the establishment of the government. We'll go back to that a bit later. As far as I understood that statement of yours, soon after the government was established and after you were appointed minister of the interior, you went to Sid?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was already in August 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was this man by the name of Slobodan Grahovac there according to our information?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You met him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he was? Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him for the first time in Sid, and he told me that he had come to help me with certain things that I was supposed to do, and that he would be there as long as it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was a member of some leadership, some war command, or under your command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say he was under my command, because had it be the case, I would have called him and I would have asked for him to come. However, since that was not the case and he didn't come there at my insistence and at my request, I understood him to be someone who was responsible to someone else to whom he reported about whatever it was that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, perhaps later or even at that time, what his prior engagements were, what he did before?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any of his own people there, some assistants, some personnel of his own? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was another man with him, his name was Dusan Filipovic, who was always with him. And this man was someone that I also saw for the first time then. I hadn't seen him ever before. I did have occasion to exchange a couple of words with him, but he never told me who he was, what he was doing there, and so on. Simply they were installed there, as it were, and I didn't really mind it, but it wasn't really a pleasant thing to have people around you you didn't know much about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had any contacts with the Territorial Defence from Serbia, the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't really know much about what they did. They didn't reveal a lot. And they would go away, but then there would always be one of them who would stay behind. And then they would take turns, the other would go and the first one would stay. So, in fact, it was as if they were there to watch or observe our actions, that they were monitoring what we were doing, to see what we were saying and whether we were actually implementing what had been agreed. And as for me, I consider that there was one man that deserved respect and I had to obey his orders, that was our agreement, and that was our president, Mr. Goran Hadzic, who told me: You will go to Sid because there are Serbian villages on that side that are surrounded. They cannot reach Sid. They have a lot of difficulties with procuring medicines, selling the harvest that had already been completed, so do see, with the military, that they help them to pass through the area and get to Sid peacefully and also to return, to get back home on a convoy that was there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the way I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in fact, am I correct to conclude that you were in Sid, in fact, just to take care of civilian affairs; in other words, to ensure that the Serbian people who lived in Western Srem could satisfy their basic needs, food and other necessities?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, that was the brunt of my work. There were also problems because there were people who didn't want to wait for the convoy and they would set out for Sid on their own. They would be captured and disappear. And there was quite a number of people who disappeared at that time. We never learned anything about their fate, where they were, what they were doing, or what had happened with them. So this was one of those important issues that I had to deal with, but sometimes -- and sometimes we did have opportunities to react and do something about it, but in most cases we didn't. But in effect, I was there because there were these people who were in a ghetto and they couldn't really get to Sid. It wasn't all that close. They would have to get through four or five Croatian villages, so getting to Sid was not an easy task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to wrap up, while you were in Sid, you didn't have any tasks that had anything to do with military issues or with, for instance, reception of volunteers or sending of military units or procurement for the military of, let's say, weapons or uniforms and so on, would you agree with me? Is that the correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, the army was in Sid, and all the tasks that I had I would have to report to Ljubisa Petrovic [as interpreted] and Subotic. They were colonels of the army. I had to discuss this with them and tell them what my plans for the day were. But as far as those who would come from elsewhere, I didn't have any weapons. I couldn't promise that I could procure that for them. There was a large warehouse in Sid where these people actually got their uniforms and were then assigned to various areas. I had absolutely nothing to do with that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "I" or "we," do you mean the Ministry of the Interior of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The entire ministry had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one final thing: I believe that in the transcript we have the name of "Ljubisa Petrovic." Did you say "Petrovic" or "Petkovic"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I said Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From your statement, where you talk about the arming of Serbs at this time, I concluded that there were three stages in all of that, and you will tell me whether I'm mistaken or not. At the beginning, these village guards or village patrols only had their own personal weapons, perhaps one or two persons would have it. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the incident in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, a certain quantity of weapons were brought there and then it turned out that they were outdated and even out of commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't know, I think maybe this was given to us just so that we would be appeased, that we would have some weapon in our hands. But, in fact, we were cheated because we received something that couldn't be used at all. So it was as if we hadn't received anything because it was useless. Of what we did see, 99 per cent was not working and couldn't be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the third stage was after the arrival of the Yugoslav Army, when they distributed weapons according to their own criteria, they distributed the weapons to people of their own choice?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when the army arrived, they recruited younger more capable men who were willing and ready to pick up arms, and this is how the weapons were distributed. However, we had nothing to do with that and we had absolutely no influence over whatever they were doing, and it was done the way it was done, without our assistance. And I believe that no one from that same government or those staffs, I don't believe that any of those people had any influence on that or that they could have done anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this process of weapons distribution by the JNA began sometime in June 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the weapons were in working order?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could learn and as far as I could see, these were almost new weapons, completely. They were in order, they worked, and there were no problems with them. If I can just add, this would not have happened had there not been a major incident between Tovarnik village and Divaca [phoen] village where the army was attacked and some five or six soldiers were killed and a lot of materiel was destroyed, or, rather, a large number of vehicles were disabled. And after this, the events that we've described occurred and that's how it was started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you one more thing: At the time when the crisis was already evident, when Croatia wanted to withdraw from Yugoslavia, when there were people who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia or not stay in Yugoslavia, so is it correct that people in general - either in Croatia or Serbia - didn't really know what the reaction of the central authorities would be, for instance, the army, the presidency, the presidency of the Republic of Serbia and so on, if Croatia was to take that action? Or what would happen if there was an attack on Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. And that's what actually frightened us, because we realised, we knew that our lives and the lives of our families were at stake and everything else, and we would just wait for the evening news to hear the latest, whether anything else had happened and so on. And at that point there were problems because many people had -- various people had various perspectives, and we didn't know whom we could trust and believe. It was very difficult to wait and see what our fate would be, but we all felt that it won't be good. There were a lot of examples, especially in Vukovar, where we knew - because this had been checked - where there had been instances where a person who was released from hospital, for instance, there was a man, I believe his name was Sava, I can't remember his last name, he was slaughtered in the street as if he was a chicken. This happened to him and to a couple of other people who themselves had no idea why this happened but it did. And, of course, no one was willing to go to work anymore, no one felt safe walking around. And in addition, I was afraid that in Serbia, too, it wasn't clear what was wanted, what the objective was, and we didn't know what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, people usually tried, through various people, from the authorities, the police, the army, the personal contacts they had somewhere, they tried to get some information, but even then, if they got it, it wasn't reliable. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very clear to us, and we had meetings amongst ourselves and we received a lot of information that we couldn't believe, because we thought everybody was just saying things that were convenient to them personally. And they often wanted to calm us down, pacify us, persuade us that we could sleep soundly, but we just knew it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Goran Hadzic was also among those who were trying desperately to get some reliable information and did he have any success?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he tried in every possible way to get some reliable information, to get the truth, and I know he had a very difficult time, perhaps the hardest time of anyone, because everybody was looking at him with great expectations. And we waited eagerly for every meeting to hear from him what was going on and ask him if we could really believe what we were hearing. I know that he had a very hard time. He was in a very difficult position because I think he, himself, could not believe the things he was being told and he didn't know what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the information he had was also not reliable and you couldn't take it for granted?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was his deputy and we shared the good and the bad for a long time, but there were often moments when I didn't believe what he was saying either because I thought he had been deceived and that the things that he was told and that he was conveying to us were simply not true. Not because I was doubting his sincerity and honesty to us but because I was doubting what he had been told to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were suspicious about his sources and the people who provided him with that information originally?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no one we could trust, no one who was able to give us reliable information and guarantee that what we were fearing would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you were in Sid, you said it was very difficult to travel to Erdut to attend cabinet meetings, and this entire communication was very complicated until the easier road through Vukovar was liberated. Tell me, how many cabinet meetings did you attend from the moment when you moved to Sid in August 1991 until the 10th or the 20th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very long road for me to travel and not even that belt towards Erdut that we took was safe. I would usually get in touch with the government secretary to find out about the agenda, and I always asked, "What is so important? Do I really have to be there?" There are many meetings that I couldn't get to, and there were meetings where I had to go because my report was important and everybody else wanted to hear what was going on, what the situation was like, et cetera, because I was the only representative of the government behind Vukovar in the direction of Sid, in that area where the majority population was Croat but there were also two or three encircled Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately how many meetings you attended? I know it was a long time ago but your answer would be valuable.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: You know, I don't know anymore how many meetings were held overall, and I cannot say with certainty how many meetings I attended and how many I failed to attend because I could easily get it wrong. It was just too long ago. And in the meantime, I had major health problems and I lost some memories, like I had slept through some of these periods. So I don't know how many meetings I attended, but I was active and I wanted to participate in all that was going on. But I'm really sorry, I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From your answer to the previous question, I see that when you were informed that a cabinet meeting was pending you inquired about the agenda and depending on that you would decide whether to go or not.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that people were most anxious to know about the situation in your area, in Western Srem, and you would go to the cabinet meeting to inform the others.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And speaking of the situation in Western Srem, they were interested in the affairs that you were sent there to handle, the civilian affairs, the supplies to the population, and the safe passage to and from Sid. Was that usually the topic of your briefing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since we had the minister of agriculture, he was supposed to cover that area, but we had an understanding that he would cover the area where he was based, Eastern Slavonia; whereas I covered Srem in all aspects that I could handle and tried to provide to the people with all they needed and help them do whatever they had to do because we had no factories, we had no corn silos to place all the corn that we had, and the wheat. We had no food processing plants. But we had to make do without it. People had to receive their old age pensions and the workers had to receive their wages. There were many, many problems we were constantly facing. And whenever I went, of course, I would reiterate these problems and present them to the session. For instance, if we had a problem with that road which was our connection with Serbia, that had to be dealt with because after two days it turned into a major problem. Also sick people had to go see a doctor, and they would have to stay in a hospital in Serbia because they couldn't get back. We were the government for the Slavonia and Baranja region and we had to take care of all these things and report back as to what needed to be done and what we were able to do. We couldn't just take part of one area and give it preferences. We had to cover the entire region and I believe we were successful, in a large measure, in providing to the people what they needed. Also at these meetings I could hear what was going on in other areas and what our plans were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Ministry of the Interior of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was established, some police stations were set up as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were these police stations? I know about Dalj and Borovo -- sorry -- yes, yes, Dalj and Borovo.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Dalj and Borovo were the first stations to be set up because that was the first area to be liberated. And it was very important to have this police station, for the police to be active also in the villages because there was always the possibility of looting and robberies. It doesn't matter by whom, Serbs or Croats or Hungarians. It's the same thing as in peacetime. People would take advantage of the circumstances and their positions to perpetrate such things, so this had to be prevented. Also people came with complaints against individuals who were bent on crime, and of course the police had to get involved and do their job properly. Very soon, the Ministry of Justice became operative and the courts began doing their work in co-operation with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. Since you were in Sid, what kind of communication did you have with, for example, the police station in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was there for the opening of the police station in Dalj and the police station in Borovo Selo. But later on when I was in Sid, I received reports from the people from the ministry who were stationed in Dalj or Borovo Selo, and I heard information about the latest developments or incidents. I did not communicate directly with the commanders of these stations, but I had my own people who worked at the recently formed ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these people you are referring to had communication with the commanders of the police stations, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Their job was to visit them regularly and keep themselves informed. I also had very experienced career police officers I was in touch with who knew their job perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the SUP of Vukovar was also based in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also have contact with the chief of SUP in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not for a long time because with the fall of Vukovar it all moved to Vukovar. It was no longer in Dalj. But I did have contact because a large part of Vukovar was liberated precisely on my side, on the side where I was based, with the majority Serb population. And there also I had a couple of men who went into the field and who informed me regularly, on a daily basis, about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know about this SUP Vukovar that was based in Dalj before Vukovar fell. I mean that part of the city that was majority Serb. If I understood you correctly, your ministry received reports from the police stations in Dalj and Borovo Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I received reports from men employed in the ministry in Dalj, Boro Zemunic [phoen] and Mr. Drzajic who worked in the Ministry of the Interior, and if anything happened, they would call me and say, We have a problem in such and such a place. Their assignment was to go on working as if I were with them and to call me urgently if I was needed and then I would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was interested in something else. The ministry, not you personally, but the Ministry of the Interior had its men in Dalj and they received regular reports from the SUP Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they also received reports from the police stations in Borovo Selo in Dalj; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had a good contact with your people from the MUP in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you spoke quite a lot about Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he came did you know what position he occupied in Serbia, in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I didn't. In fact, it was quite a while before we first met because I was already in Sid. But we did meet. I believe it was at a government session in Erdut which he attended to. And before that, there had been a meeting where we had decided that not a single member of the government would enter a cabinet session armed. There were no formal introductions. I was just told: This is Badza. And when we were already sitting there at the meeting, all the ministers were seated, when Badza came in in armour, armed, and when the meeting was about to begin, I asked: "What is this all about? I was told that nobody could bring in a weapon to the meeting. I see that you are armed. You are supposed to leave your weapon outside. There are men who will keep it for you because you are not in danger here. You don't need a weapon." To which he said, "I can come in with a weapon. I don't have to leave it outside. You just don't know who I am." And I answered: "I've heard who you are, but whoever you are, you have to leave your weapon outside." And this exchange took a few minutes, and then the other members of the government got involved. And when he realised that what he had done was improper, he left and he didn't come back to this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that your first encounter?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was our first encounter. And after that we were formally introduced, because I had been told that I had to keep in touch with him because he was from the MUP of Serbia and he had come to help us out with handling all that we had to handle and set up our police and defence and everything. And I said okay, it's not a problem, but I had a feeling right away that he and I would not be able to have a good co-operation because he was not a local. He was not one of us. He didn't understand the situation we were in. And the way he saw it, he was a man from Belgrade, a very important person, and he thought that with his move to our district he lost some of his authority and importance because he was no longer just giving orders. That's not the way we worked. We made decisions together as a government as to what we were going to do, and he probably didn't like that. We had our first talk and from that talk I came away thinking that we would have a hard time working together. And indeed it was not long before he asked for my resignation, and he asked it from Goran personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he arrived, do you know if he took over the police or the police stations? Did he place them under his control and command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It couldn't have been done that way because when we formed the government, every minister was given a portfolio, a clear set of tasks, and a clear reporting line. We had to be all accountable to Goran. We couldn't make any important moves without him. But neither I nor the other ministers believed that he was able to do whatever he pleased. And let me tell you, that meeting where he asked for my resignation, he didn't manage because all the other ministers wanted me to stay in my place. That happened at the first meeting. At the second meeting, yes, I did talk to President Hadzic. He said that it would be a good idea for me to take a different portfolio, such as trade or something, to resolve the problem. I didn't agree. And then we had many more meetings. It was very, very unpleasant. And finally I said, "No problem. I'll withdraw. Let my job be taken over by whoever is willing," because I was by that time very resentful. And even another minister, Boro Milenkovic, left that government, saying, "I don't want to work in a cabinet where others give orders and do as they please."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, you said something here. You said that all members of the government were responsible to Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you and all the ministers and Hadzic were elected by the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all elected by the National Assembly, but Goran Hadzic was the first one to be elected, the prime minister. So according to this hierarchy we were supposed to report to him and he was the one that we communicated with. Not everybody can complain to the National Assembly. It was Goran who --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because according to my information, none of the ministers reported to Goran Hadzic or submitted any kind of reports to Goran Hadzic at all. That's why I'm asking you. If I understood you correctly, everybody said what they had to say at government sessions but they did not submit reports to Hadzic and they did not report to him for their work, according to my information. Are you claiming that ministers reported to him in terms of what it was that they were doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, every government meeting was, of course, opened by Mr. Hadzic. That is to say, he would open the meeting and also he had the right to ask what was going on in my department. Also, I was duty-bound to say either that everything was all right or if there was something wrong to say that, too. That's the way it was for me. I respected the hierarchy involved. If the National Assembly had elected him as prime minister, and I know that the prime minister can replace a minister or present a proposal to have him dismissed or whatever, I don't understand -- I mean, well, does that mean that all the ministers would just be working on their own? I mean, did they not report to him? That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, at government meetings ministers would present their problems, the problems that they had - if I understand you correctly - and then that was discussed there, whether something should be done or not be done, whether it was being done properly or not? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in that sense you believe that this means reporting to Hadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I heard all of that sort of in passing, and people said to me that Badza was in charge of the Ministry of the Interior, Badza is the one who has the main say in the Ministry of Defence. I wasn't surprised about the Ministry of Defence because Ilija Kojic was appointed there and he was with the Vukovar police, and I mean, well - how do I put this? - he had quite a bit in common with Badza. I did not. But I found this strange, that a person who had come and who was out there in the field, that he should be minister of defence without knowing the people there, which is particularly important; that is to say, the local people, the local population, irrespective of ethnicity. There were people there, say, Ruthenians, who did not know who they should join, so they were split up. Then there were also some other people who were not in favour of what the Croatian authorities were doing although they were ethnic Croats. But that was not their objective and they were not in favour of that. So a man who cannot decide at a given point in time whether that was good or not. So that is something that bothered me quite a bit because, as I said, quite simply if I know, well, not only the people there but each and every foot of the land there, I grew up there, I lived there for 45 years, and you arrive there as someone who is there for the first very first time, you don't know anyone, you don't know anything, and you're taking over? For me that was a very bad thing, but that's the way it was and that is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you heard that he was commander --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- of the Territorial Defence? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? Let me ask you something: When speaking to the Office of the Prosecutor - and I see that there were quite a few of these conversations - did you ever say that to them, that you had heard that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember all the conversations that took place, but I know that he was the one and that is probably something that was well known, that he was the person who was in command and who actually commanded the operations that were carried out in the area of Slavonia and Baranja -- well, again, you see, I find this a bit strange. The commander of the Territorial Defence at that time -- you see, when we established that government, the army was there, as you know, and on several occasions we had the opportunity of hearing that for as long as the army was there, there was no civilian defence or protection and we can only have those things that the army agrees to done. And now, appointing a Badza commander of the defence, that is something that I found sort of unclear. Do you see what I'm saying? For example, the Territorials, the volunteers, everybody, they were all within the JNA, except for Arkan, who was in his own place and he did not answer to anyone. But everybody else, as far as I know, had to be subordinated to the army; that is to say, the commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one question: Did you know what the relationship was between Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and the JNA? Was he subordinated to the JNA like others?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," did you not know or was he not subordinated?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that he was not subordinated to them because his co-ordination and the co-ordination of the army was very poor; that is to say, on this side where I was, that is to say, Western Srem, I mean, he didn't even come there. He didn't know what was being done or how it was being done. That is one thing. Secondly, let me say this straight away, in order to have this known here, the side that Radovan Stojicic was on, the population is 80 per cent Serb, and I believe that it wasn't really necessary at all to have any kind of major war operations or something like that. However, nothing had still happened in Vukovar. But where the army had arrived, there were four Serb villages and some villages that had about 30 per cent Serb population, all the rest were Croats. So that was it. The commanders in Brsadin, Bobota, Trpinja, Vera, Pacetin, Klisa, and the rest, I don't know that were purely Serb. I don't know what that meant. So this is really what mattered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, sorry for that. I have a small question to ask to the witness before moving to another topic. Witness, paragraph 36, you said that Arkan didn't obey anyone. What does that mean? Who did he get his orders from? What was he doing there? You said that he obeyed anyone [as interpreted], what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, this is the way it was. Arkan arrived in Erdut. I know that the prime minister, Goran Hadzic, and we and the ministers did not decide about him coming there, but he did show up in Erdut. And let me tell you this: He was not with the army. He was not with us. He was the one who operated as he wished. As far as I know, he did not answer to any one of us. Also, he didn't answer to anyone in Belgrade. He was a man who just worked on his own and that's how he behaved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he did not report to Belgrade. Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then no one was able to stop him or to do anything because he did not report to you or to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Arkan had his own unit in Erdut consisting of about 300 men. He went into action on his own, without agreeing with the army, without agreeing with us or anybody else. He did it on his own. And most often, most often, these operations were you carried out according to his own scenario, as he had envisaged things. That's the way he did them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, would this be an appropriate moment for the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll be back at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bogunovic, you've said that you know that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was not under the command of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. However, I would like to clear up one thing with you because I had the impression you meant that part of the Yugoslav People's Army that operated south of Vukovar, in that area where you were. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know if he might have had a relationship or communication with the units that were north of Vukovar in that area, as they called it, Operative Group North?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, when he arrived in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, brought a unit with him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I knew about four or five men who arrived with him. I did not know the others. I didn't know who they were, what they were, and I never had occasion to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see my information is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can see 1D2337, please, but it should not be emitted to the public and to the witness. The number is 1D2337.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the rules we have here, I can't show you that document, but I will put to you the main points that are of interest to us. Namely, from this document, paragraph 7, one unit made up of 30 men arrived at Dalj on 24 September 1991. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they took over police affairs in Dalj. It's written in paragraph 9 of this same statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am standing because I believe the witness said he didn't know anything about these men arriving, and so the follow-up question seems to have been answered. The witness says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't say -- I'm asking him about the Dalj police station and the overtaking of the work of this specific police station in Dalj. It is in period when he was minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's see what the answer is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, do you know that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and his men took over police business in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they stayed there and organised police stations in Bijelo Brdo, Erdut, Borovo Selo, as we see in paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know about Borovo Selo. I was involved in the establishment of that station. As for Bijelo Brdo and the others, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- are you continuing this line of question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask the witness. You said: "I know about Borovo Selo." What do you know about Borovo Selo? The question was: Was it taken over by - what is the name again? - Stojicic's -- Badza -- Stojicic's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the police stations in Dalj and Borovo Selo were the first ones to be set up, and they had already been established when Mr. Stojicic arrived, so I don't see what he would be establishing there upon his arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you know that Borovo Selo police station was taken over by Badza's men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one of your statements I read - and if you want me to refresh your memory, I'll find it and read it - you said that the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was a virtual government. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clear that up a little. Did you mean that it did not have such authority as to be respected by those who should have respected it or what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the people expected from us certain things. For them, we were the people whom they knew and believed, and that's what we tried to do. First of all, the army appeared in the Srem and Baranja region, especially Western Srem, and they always said: We do not recognise civilian authorities. As long as we are here, there will be military authority. So we could not do anything without them, without their approval and knowledge. We just couldn't do anything without first asking their permission. So we did have a government but that government was not able to decide in very important matters that concerned the people and everything that happened in that region because the army was there. Second, there was Arkan and Arkan had his own vision. There was Badza, and now I hear before this honourable Tribunal that Badza changed police stations, established police stations, that he was a war commander, that he was involved in combat, so I believe that we were squeezed out of our own jobs. I went to my own village where my family lives and where Mr. Sljivancanin was the commander, and every time I went there I had to report to him first before going to my house because that's the rule that he had introduced. So I practically didn't even have freedom of movement as a native of that area, as a local resident. And that's what I meant. The government that had been appointed did not, in fact, decide anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one piece of information that is slightly different about the work of that government. According to that piece of information, the government was able to decide, but it couldn't put anything into practice.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were not able to do much and we were supposed to work in the best interests of the people, but the people could not count on us for that. For instance, we had a minister of agriculture, who was very important, and he couldn't secure for the commodities produced in Slavonia and Baranja to be exported to Serbia. We had cornmeal and sugar beet, and we needed to be paid for that in order to be able to pay out the wages and the old age pensions because that was a very long period, and we did not have savings or money accumulated for people to go on working without being paid for two years. So we were supposed to be taking care of the population. They were supposed to feel that somebody's taking care about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if my information is correct: That the government was able to make decisions but it could not implement them on the ground because it didn't have the agencies, the authorities who would do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, among other things, something about the context that members of the government and Mr. Hadzic had in Serbia. You said they discussed various matters with various people in Vojvodina, in Serbia, and that you know about that. So would you tell me: What were these issues that they normally discussed with people from Serbia, and what did Hadzic himself discuss? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we would usually go to President Hadzic, because he had the largest circle of contacts, asking for his help. I'll give you my example: For instance, the Ministry of the Interior established two police stations and then continued to set up others, and I didn't know anyone in Novi Sad, so I asked him to accompany me when I was going there to ask for weapons and uniforms and vehicles, everything that a police force needs. So we went to Novi Sad together, we had discussions there, and I received a batch of 200 uniforms that I took to Krajina to distribute to the employees of the police so that they be properly dressed, that they could be distinguished as policemen, and that people should recognise them as the men who are responsible for law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said you were taking these uniforms to Krajina, you mean Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or that later Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking only about the Slavonia, Baranja area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, what were other major problems that made your government contact the government of Serbia? What were the most important problems?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: We had meetings in Erdut and in Novi Sad with them. We focused on contacts in Vojvodina because they were easier to reach. So the ministers of finance met first, then the ministers of agriculture, then the ministers of trade, those were the ministries that were important in terms of our trade co-operation between the Slavonia, Baranja area and Serbia. And our job was to collect payment for our exports. And we needed people like the minister of energy because many villages did not have electricity and people couldn't live normally, so they worked together on getting the electrical supply repaired and installed in every village so that people could go on with their normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the topic of these meetings between people from Vojvodina - that is to say, Serbia - and your people were civilian affairs, such as energy, trade, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Only civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your estimate - although I believe you've already said it in your statement, but let us reiterate it - do you think that any one of you from the government, beginning with Hadzic down, was able to give any instructions or orders to Radovan Stojicic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I am sure that nobody was able to give orders to him. The people who were close to him, who were around him, had to obey. And I mean specifically President Hadzic, who would often receive visits from Stojicic who barged into his office whenever he liked, and I could see on Hadzic that he didn't like what he had been told and that he wasn't willing to do that, especially since it often ran counter to what we wanted to do and what we had agreed to do. Our life was easier, much easier, when there were no Badzas and no Arkans. We were able to talk together normally, we knew very well what was going in every corner of our region, and we could agree easily. When they arrived, we made one decision, it's vetoed by Badza. We make another decision, it's refused by Arkan or the army. And to be quite honest, there were threats as well, threats of physical violence. Those were not people with whom you could play games or with whom you can have a normal discussion. If you failed to do as they said, your fate was pretty much sealed. And to be frank, we had to worry about saving our own skins because our people needed us, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us everything, since you said that there were some orders there or, rather, decisions that Badza didn't like or Arkan? What kind of decisions were they?
