What was it that you decided that they didn't like? If you cannot remember a specific decision -- of course, it would be a good thing if you could remember, but if not, could you tell us what they were like? In what field? Did they have to do with trade, finance, I don't know, police affairs or I don't know what?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'll start with the police. The police had to do what Badza had thought. We knew the people who worked in the police. We knew people, irrespective of faith, ethnicity, regardless of what they were like or what they were not like. There were some Croats who were oriented towards Yugoslavia, also there were such Hungarians and Ruthenians. However, these people did not see it that way. So our people were bothered by orders like that and this kind of treatment of other people. So first the police could not work as they were supposed to work, as we were used to. Or, for example, they'd bring in a man who was certainly not guilty. This was a serious man who knew what he was doing. However, we could not exercise any influence. Also, as for this finance and everything else, it wasn't always like why things are going here, why they are going there, why are you doing this, or why are you doing that, although we tried to have contact with important people in the government of Vojvodina so that they could decide what suited us, but that did not always work out. Also this finance and also the military -- well, there were a lot of things, actually, that did not suit us and were not very convenient for us and things did not go as we had planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please try to be a bit more succinct. I see from your answer that part of it had to do with certain pre-trial proceedings or some other proceedings against certain persons that were arrested by Badza and his men and you thought that these people should not have been arrested. Did I understand what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then this other situation that has to do with purely financial transactions. You wanted to sell goods. For instance, you wanted to deal with one particular company in Serbia and they thought that you should have been doing business with somebody else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to hear more about this first thing that we discussed, these arrests. Can you tell us, if I understood you correctly, did they do that without asking any one of you, without consulting any one of you? I mean, they did not ask you first whether somebody should be arrested or not? Or did they not simply ask anyone in the government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to tell you that things happened and they did not suit any one of us except for the person who thought that that's the way things should be done. Let me give you an example. Arkan, without asking anyone, although President Hadzic was not far away from there, he did not consult him at all. He did not consult anyone else. He took three or four men out of the police station in Dalj, they never returned, and nobody knew what happened to them. For us, that was -- well, we could not understand that something like that could be done. And finally, you know what? What made us go on? We thought what would happen if others did everything that they wanted them to do, whereas we wanted to work for the benefit of all, so that things would go well for us and all of those around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you're speaking about this concrete case, did that happen -- I mean, do you know when that happened? More specifically, what the month was or something like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's been a while. It was August or September when I received a letter from a commander of a police station who had been dismissed by Badza. Badza said to him, "You're wrong for that," and that's it. You know, that's how it was. That's when it happened. In my view, everyone who did not think along the same lines as Badza and Arkan had to be dismissed, and then Badza, Arkan, and the others would appoint people to these positions themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the name of this police station commander was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Cizmic, if I remember correctly. I may be right, but please don't take my word for this with 100 per cent certainty. This is what I seem to remember, that that was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P115.111. [In English] I don't know if it is confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is. It should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see it on the screen? This document is dated the 18th of October, 1991. I would now like to ask you to read it to yourself, and then once you're done, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Zivanovic please turn on his other microphone that is close to the screen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened? Are you familiar with this thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that right after that, I think that literally on the following day the chief of SUP was replaced, the chief of SUP of Vukovar with his headquarters in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, did you make this decision to have him replaced?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't even know that he would be replaced. I didn't know about this that happened. But later on I heard what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anything was done there? Have you read the whole document -- oh, yes, it's just one page. Yes. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, ultimately nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there is another page so I'd like to ask you to read that as well.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you the following: First of all, did you see from this report that some offices were demolished during this protest?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, do you remember -- or, rather, do you know what the reason was, why, immediately after this protest, the chief of SUP of Vukovar with headquarters in Dalj was dismissed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody had to be dismissed after that and this man was the casualty or the scapegoat, and that was it. Although he did the least of all. It didn't happen in the station. It happened in the area where Arkan operated and where Badza was or, rather, where -- you see where these tank units were, where all this happened. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you spoke about a crime at a brick factory. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the crime or is it something different?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I see here that it has to do with 40 men. These are people from Serbia, Sonta. These are people -- these were people who were farming near Beli Manastir and they were transported there, about 15 of them. Among these 15 there was a man with the same surname as mine. He was executed there and he also went missing there. His father kept trying to find out what happened. I didn't know either, but later on I found out that that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you spoke about the group from Beli Manastir in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the first time I hear of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. You've already said that apparently he did not answer to anyone either in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or in Serbia. In your statement I've noticed you said that technically he was under the control of the MUP, under Badza's command.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't under Badza's command. As far as I was able to see, they did have understandings, they did talk, but Badza couldn't do anything about Arkan. Arkan was there with 3- or 400 men and at that time he wasn't listening to anyone. Badza might have tried. Maybe they even had an agreement at some point. But Badza's orders were not to work with Arkan. That much is certain. His job was different. I'm sure it was not on the orders of his superiors in Serbia. Arkan was unto himself. He didn't acknowledge Badza or the government or anyone else. He did exactly as he wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How is something like that possible? How is it possible to have 3-, 400 men under your command and not be controlled by anyone, the authorities in Serbia or the regional authorities, the army, or the police?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Arkan certainly had protection from somebody in Belgrade. That's indisputable. And he did what he did as he pleased, and I wouldn't accept that the police would let him do these things without consulting anyone. What he did in Erdut and what he did later, he did all that at his own initiative. I am quite sure that he was a freelancer. He didn't accept Badza's suggestions or anybody else's advice. And I believe that nobody was able to control that man at that time. He did exactly as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you believe that even the army was unable to rein him in?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that. I witnessed a couple of encounters where he spoke very insolently and even insulted military officers. Let me not repeat the words he used here when speaking to majors, captains, colonels, but he told them in so many words that he was not going to share anything with them or listen to their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we need to go back to this document that I showed you a moment ago, this report about the incident in Dalj. You've seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have -- sorry, may we have P115.111. It's on the screen, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that document in front of you, page 1? As far as I can see, these about 300 members of TO Dalj, brought Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, to that meeting and required various explanations, and then he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic is speaking so far away from the microphone that we really have a hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't understand your explanation, your explanation that nobody was able to rein him in; whereas here we see that members of a local territorial force persuaded him, convincingly enough, to come to their meeting and make himself accountable.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I accept that he came to that meeting and told them what they wanted to hear. I'm quite sure that he didn't give them any explanations, but I'm also sure that the very next day he continued doing exactly as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that he accepted their invitation, if we can put it that way, and it says they ushered him out at gunpoint. That's what we see in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot believe that because you can only carry him out feet first if he didn't want to go somewhere. You could only kill him and nothing else. That's the kind of man he was. And from the little I knew him, that's the way he was and that's the way he stayed until the end of his life. He certainly didn't accept it at gunpoint, because I don't know how many men were there, but if there had been any, even the smallest skirmish, none of them would have gotten out of their alive. So they probably came to some sort of understanding that he would go there and talk to those people, but he certainly didn't promise anyone that he would change his ways, and he continued doing exactly the same things. If not in Dalj, then he continued doing them in other places. And that's the way it was until the very end. And I'm sure that those people who saw that he was building something and organising something, nobody even thought of trying to stop him because that's the way he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic turn on the microphone he's speaking into.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning this answer you've just given, it's based on your assumptions and your conclusions? You actually don't know what happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you just one thing: Our government did the best it could to help those people there, but we noticed that even Badza was interfering, not to mention Arkan. All of us who went there, and especially those who had offices there, had to watch their every word and every step and had to be very, very careful not to offend those men. We had information that somebody was supposed to intercept Slavko Dokmanovic when he travelled to his own village and kill him. You can simply not imagine now the kinds of things we went through every day in that time. We never knew if we would get back home alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just see if this is a mistake in the interpretation or in the transcript. It was said that Goran -- you mentioned Goran, but I think that was not recorded. You said that he had to watch his every step. Could you just repeat that passage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: He had to watch every step he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "he," you mean Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from this I infer that he was somehow followed, watched by Arkan and Badza and their men, is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he knows these things better than I. But it's not only him. All of us were aware that his every word and his every step were monitored, were closely followed. There were men around him who watched from up close and reported to whom they had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he and the other members of the government were watched and followed, I conclude from that that these people had no trust in either him or the government. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: To them we were all suspicious, and almost no one was free in their actions. There were perhaps certain things that we worked on that were not very interesting to them, but if they were interested in something, we had to be very careful what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you also spoke about Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, and I saw this in your statement, according to my information, Goran Hadzic and Jovica Stanisic did not know each other in 1991. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Whether they knew each other, I'm not sure, but I don't see why they would have to know each other at that time. I saw Jovica Stanisic a couple of times, but I know that that man never came our way, to our area, and I never heard him talk about us and I didn't have the impression he was interested in us. I cannot be 100 per cent sure that they didn't know each other, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke in your statement about Vojislav Seselj and his visit to Vukovar. You remember?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you: You were there when he visited once?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you talk to him about anything?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in Negoslavci, and my orders were to take him to Vukovar so that he could inspect the situation there. And at that moment, the people with howitzers were around Vukovar and everybody around them wanted them to leave. Nothing was happening. People were standing there, waiting. Morale was very low. And he had been sent there to change something, to get things moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, he was sent to boost the morale of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Had the army been given notice of his arrival?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were any officers around when he came?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when he reached those first soldiers who were working on the maintenance of the howitzers, he stopped to talk to them, he said, "How are things going?" They said things were bad. They said they didn't know why they were there, what's going on, and he tried to explain that they were needed. And he went from left to right, from the first howitzer to the last, saying that things would change and that they need to stay there because things were what they were but they were needed. And he promised them that things would change, and he said that he would come and visit at least another five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether previously, before he came to these positions, whether he had been in Negoslavci where the command was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. That visit to Negoslavci and this arrival and then that departure to Vukovar, I mean, that was at the very front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, on that day he was in both Negoslavci and in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether in Negoslavci he saw any JNA officers? Did they know that he had come at all?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They must have known. It would be impossible for him to come without any of the officers knowing. Now, whether they wanted to talk to him or not, that's a different matter. But I did not notice anyone talking to him then, anyone well known engaging in dialogue with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had come with a security detail?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only two of his pals, whatever, came with him. He did not have a security detail at all. He got a security detail only in Negoslavci and then they accompanied him to Vukovar and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: These were soldiers and the TO. Actually, mostly TO, mostly TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the TO was under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said in your statement that there was security provided to the government -- rather, there were persons who guarded government buildings in Erdut. And then if the members of the government travelled somewhere, they travelled with them as body-guards of sorts. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you said that Stevo Bogic was in charge of that security for the government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have -- actually, Stevo Bogic was the deputy prime minister. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, this security of the government was there round-the-clock. They took turns. They worked in shifts. They worked there, slept there. They worked in shifts. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Also according to my information, there were about ten of them, although often they would change. Some left and others came, but there were about ten of them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: About ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Stevo Bogic was also elected deputy prime minister by the Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he could have been dismissed like all of you if the Assembly decided to do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you spoke about the Serb National Security?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the Serb National Security, is it precisely these people who provided security for the government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that primarily they were supposed to provide security for the buildings and rooms where the government was and where Goran was at the time, but also it wasn't really some kind of national security that could not move around. The army was there and, of course, the things were the way they were but they were supposed to hear about things being done. They were supposed to inform the prime minister about that kind of thing, at least to a certain degree. They weren't really security people the way they exist nowadays. They were there for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, they could not carry out the work that the state security would have been doing? Is that what you mean? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they certainly could not. In times like that, in a situation like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to clarify this. I understand that they were securing the government premises and also providing security for government members when they travelled. But this information, what did you mean when they received information? What kind of information would this be, of what nature? What was this supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to be what was happening in other parts of the Slavonia, Baranja region. Whether something was happening somewhere, whether something was wrong, or whether other things were happening, say, things that the president was supposed to know about. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know why I find this unclear? These were people who would work in, say, two-hour shifts, providing security for the government day and night, round-the-clock. Of course they would spend certain intervals sleeping as well. So they were in the Erdut all the time. How could they get information about what was happening throughout the region when they were not moving about, unless they had some special kind of people who were sending information to them? As far as I understood your answer, it wasn't that kind of service. It wasn't like state security.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't, but somebody had to be told about what was going on in some place where, I mean, the army was or Arkan or the police or I don't know. People had to know, at least to a degree, so that the prime minister would know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if they received some information about Arkan's movements or the army's movements, they were supposed to inform their superior? I suppose Bogic, Stevo, who would convey that to Hadzic; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can understand some of this, but why was that interesting, where the army was moving at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the army but just what was happening out in the field. You see, that was very important. For instance, what happened, say, where Arkan was and other people who did something that was not supposed to be done. We thought that the president should know that and that he should not be the last person to hear about this. After all, he should know. He should have the situation under his control. Let me say that I knew this, and I stand by this to this day, namely that people on the ground, when the president went somewhere, they were not thrilled if they would see Arkan and others with him. That's because people were enraged by things that happened where Arkan was. That's why this was not right. That's why we wanted our own people to escort our president, people we knew would do everything to save him and to spare him from something that was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ljuba Mudrinic was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that during the war he was the body-guard of Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, he was, but Goran knows best of all. To tell you quite frankly, I believe that he was nearby, but that he was his direct body-guard, I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Milenko Japundic [phoen] was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know who Milenko Japundic is and I know that he was devoted to the president and I know that he was on his security detail and that he was there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Mudrinic and Milenko Japundic were not in Arkan's Serb Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were from the local -- I mean, from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. They had not come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Milenko is from Osijek, but that's all the same as far as we're concerned. For us what mattered was that he was not with Arkan, in that unit, that kind of thing. Then things would be viewed differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you know these two, Mudrinic, Japundic, do you agree that they were not involved in any kind of criminal activity along the lines of what you've been saying?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that these are people who had to leave the places where they lived, and I'm sure that they were proper, that they did not have any kind of criminal record. They did what they did out of patriotism, and they wanted to be there for the president whom they protected. Honestly, I'm sure, and they would have done anything to protect him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said, among other things, that there was state security. Now I wanted us to clarify the matter. First of all, what period were you referring to when you said that there was a state security?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, state security was mentioned even while I was minister. But at the time, that did not start functioning because most of the territory was under the Croat control, so it was impossible to do things that way. After that, I believe that that was established. Couldn't be done any differently. People had to know that there was a state security that took care of what was going on, what people were saying, what was being done, and so on and so forth. And at that moment, they certainly conveyed to the president what they knew and what was heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember from some things I've seen, you were dismissed from your job first as minister and then as deputy prime minister of SBWS on the 21st December 1991. There seems to be a mistake. It was 19 December, not 21st. And I believe around that time that constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was adopted and with it all these three regions were united into one republic, Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about the state security, did you mean that period which began with the establishment of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the establishment of the MUP with both its sectors, the public security and the state security, did you mean that period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, maybe, that the MUP was then under the minister of the interior and it had these two branches: Public security and state security? And practically the boss of both was the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the minister of the interior was in the republic Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing because you were in Sid. I have information that at that time when fighting began, anyone who wanted to go to the area of Vukovar, Negoslavci, et cetera, had to have a permit from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They had to have a pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued these passes? First let me ask you, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were first issued by the army and then they handed it over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did they hand it over to you, when the Vukovar operation was already completed or when?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, the operation Vukovar was not yet finished. It was handed over to me before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean before the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Before the operation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was towards the end of September, early October. That's when we began issuing passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Early October. When you say "we," you mean --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the army no longer did that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They stopped issuing passes at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure? Because you are the only man who says that. Everyone else says exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe they issued some passes to people who came directly to see them, but they handed over this work to us regarding people who were travelling back and forth to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough in my question. You were talking about those people who were living in villages in Western Srem, and when they came to Sid you gave them these passes so they could go back home?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that's what you meant? That was your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the army issued passes to those people who went into the reserve force at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, you're overlapping and putting the interpreters in difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if somebody else wanted to travel to Vukovar at that time, a civilian, he would have to go to the army for a pass?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up one more thing concerning the incident at Lovas. You mentioned it in your statement. I can show you that document, in fact. Let me just find it. You said, among other things, that you found out later about that incident, and I wanted to ask you: Did you know that the army had carried out an inquiry there? They sized up the situation, they sent a report to the competent authorities within the military hierarchy, the military prosecutor, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard at the briefing when he went to see Colonel Petkovic and Colonel Subotic. I didn't know that thing had happened in Lovas, but I heard from them that they had sent a commission over there to inquire and the resulting material had been sent to the proper place in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, considering that you were a minister of the interior, does this indicate that at that time it was the army that was responsible for investigating and prosecuting that case?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I could not even come near that location at the time. Nobody cared that I was minister of the interior. Without the army's permission, I could not even come near.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said here for the record earlier today that every morning you reported to this Colonel Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did it look? Did you get any instructions from him as to what you should do that day, or did you get any approvals or what?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would tell me whether there would be an escort to the convoy from Negoslavci, Banovci, to Sid and back, and if anything else needed to be done, they would give me my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the JNA and the Territorial Defence liberated certain places or occupied certain places, and as they did so, they would establish military authority.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that mean that after that the civilian authorities had no longer any jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't do anything anymore, and they wouldn't even let us organise a local commune or something else that would be civilian. When we suggested it, they would say: No, you can't do anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you also said that you tried hard to stop people from leaving those villages where the Territorial Defence and JNA had taken over.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did people want to leave their villages as soon as the JNA and the TO arrived?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was not enough to liberate a village and for the army and TO to arrive. It was also necessary for people to enable to sell their goods, to buy what they needed, to go out into the fields and do their farm work, and at that moment it was not possible any longer. When they would be told that they are no longer allowed to leave their houses and go work on their farms, then people saw no other way out than to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose it would be the military authorities who were to give them this permission?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We needed people to stay in their homes. Those were not people who were any threat to the army. They simply had their farms, their houses, their livestock, the land, and they needed to work. Our problem was that we needed to keep those people from evacuating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In December 1991, as far as I'm able to see, you moved to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was your assignment given you by the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That decision was made at a cabinet session and it was suggested by President Hadzic. He said that somebody from the government should be in Ilok because 60- or 70.000 people were waiting to be accommodated there, and somebody from the government should take care of that and assign houses to family depending on the size of the house and the size of the family. And I as deputy prime minister and Vojno Susa as minister of justice and Mr. Vojnovic as minister of finance were designated to go to Ilok, and we stayed there for I don't know exactly how long but rather a long time until we had completed all this business with accommodating these people. In Ilok we also had about 2.000 Slovaks and we had to keep an eye on them too, to avoid any problems. Mr. Jan Kisgeci [phoen], who was minister of agriculture in Slobodan Milosevic's government, was particularly concerned about these people. He called every day to ask us if there were any problems, what was going on, et cetera, but we managed for all these Slovaks to stay put all the way until peaceful reintegration which happened in late 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, were there any empty houses?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were houses abandoned by the Croats who had lived earlier in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to some information we have, they left on the 17th October or the 18th, I'm not sure?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In these talks and negotiations about the departure of Croats from Ilok, did the government of SBWS play any role in these talks?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. At that time nobody asked us anything. The negotiations were led by the army and they agreed with the Croat population of Ilok. The Croats from Ilok said they wanted to leave Ilok, go to Croatia using the motorway that passes by Batkovici. Although it was not without problems. They were told that it was not a good idea, et cetera, that they should stay put. But they were adamant that they wanted to leave Serbia and go live in Croatia, except those 2.000 Slovaks who remained to live in Ilok along with a number of Croats and Hungarians in other villages around Ilok who also stayed. And we were facing another problem. By that time there were already 4.000 refugees from Backa Slavonia who were temporarily accommodated in the sports hall in Backa Palanka, and we were trying to come to an agreement with the army to make a swap so that these people could exchange their houses. And these people who were put up in the sports hall had been living there without a bathroom for eight days. Four thousand is a huge number of people. They were starting to smell. And we stayed there for another few days, but the army was unable to make a decision. And then I called up our government, explained the situation, and I said that we should move those people. And then a meeting was held in Backa Palanka and the meeting was attended by President Hadzic and by myself, and that's when I first saw Mr. Stanisic. He was also there but he didn't participate. He was just taking notes. And that's how it came about, that we moved those people to Ilok and then we set up a headquarters that handled distribution of empty houses, according to the size of the house and the size of families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What you've just described, that was in the end of 1991 and early 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there? Did you witness the departure of those people from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody could be there except the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you one letter that was sent to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D30. If we could see it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd kindly ask you to read this letter to yourself, and then I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to the letter. And please tell us once you're done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we go over the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have the second page, too. In B/C/S and English we have three pages, as far as I know. We have five pages in English, actually. [Interpretation] Yes, there is one more page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have -- thank you. Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now. You've read the letter. Did it reflect reality, the reality of what was going on then; that is to say, the 23rd of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time there was military administration in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I can see, there was not a strict separation of these powers. This letter actually asks for that, to see what the authority that you could possibly have in that situation would be. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I see that you did not even know about the criteria on the basis of which people moved into these abandoned houses and how the refugees from Western Slavonia got into these houses in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that during the first days we didn't have access to anything. We simply sat there, watched, and waited to see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time when this letter was written?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand you full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, I see that this letter asks that the Ministry of the Interior should be informed about the activity of the Ilok police station. It says here, of course, if these are civilian rather than military police forces; in other words, the government did not know of the police station that was functioning there at all. They didn't know what kind of police station it was in the first place. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation of what you said, Mr. Zivanovic, but I can imagine what it was and I thank you for it. Mr. Bogunovic, your cross-examination has not yet been completed and therefore you have to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Now because you are sworn as a witness, you cannot speak to the attorneys of either party nor discuss your testimony with anybody else. Any conversation you have with persons other than the attorneys cannot relate to the testimony that you have given here so far. So we are taking the adjournment until tomorrow. 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of April, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 25
